# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey (HTOPS)
Description: The Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey (HTOPS) is a national survey panel by the U.S. Census Bureau (Census). The purpose of the panel is to collect information on topics such as food and nutrition, transportation, employment, and education and to gather data that can be used to improve and inform future surveys. The panel will consist of individuals and households living across the U.S. who have agreed to be contacted and invited to participate in surveys.
URL: https://census.gov/programs-surveys/htops.html

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research this dataset comprehensively, starting with the official Census Bureau page and related searches.I have strong initial material. Let me dig deeper into the survey's history, partner agencies, methodology, and how the data are used and accessed.# Research Report: Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey (HTOPS)

## Executive Summary

The Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey (HTOPS) is an **experimental, high-frequency national household survey** run by the **U.S. Census Bureau** (within the Department of Commerce) under its **High-Frequency Surveys Program**. It is the direct successor to two programs: the **Household Pulse Survey (HPS)**, the Census Bureau's celebrated COVID-19 rapid-response survey (April 2020–September 2024), and the **Census Household Panel (CHP)**, a probability-based research panel (2023–2024). HTOPS collects near-real-time data on employment, food sufficiency, housing, health, transportation, education, inflation, and other emergent social and economic topics, and serves as a methodological testbed for improving Census Bureau surveys and the 2030 Census.

Your description is **largely accurate but slightly dated**: it describes HTOPS as a *panel* of households "who have agreed to be contacted," which was true of the 2025 design. **Beginning in March 2026, HTOPS transitioned from a longitudinal panel back to a cross-sectional design** with independent bi-monthly samples; the Census Bureau's current page now describes it simply as "a national survey" of randomly selected addresses. Details below.

---

## 1. Publisher and Governance

- **Publisher/sponsor:** U.S. Census Bureau (primary sponsor), Demographic Programs Directorate, under the **High-Frequency Surveys Program**. The Federal Register notices are submitted by the Department of Commerce.
- **Partner agencies:** HTOPS/HPS content is developed cooperatively with a large consortium of federal agencies, including (per the Census Bureau's own listing): Bureau of Labor Statistics, Bureau of Transportation Statistics, CDC, Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, Department of Defense, Energy Information Administration, HHS, HUD, FDA, Maternal and Child Health Bureau, National Center for Education Statistics, National Center for Health Statistics, National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases, National Endowment for the Arts, NIOSH, Office of the Surgeon General, USDA Economic Research Service, USDA Food and Nutrition Service, the White House Council of Economic Advisers, and the White House Domestic Policy Council. Other agencies may also contribute funding and sponsor topical modules.
- **Statutory authority:** Title 13, U.S. Code — variously cited as §§ 8(b), 131, 141, 182, 193, and 196 (the current respondent-facing page cites §§ 131, 141, 182, 193, 196; the OMB ICR abstract cites §§ 8(b), 141, 182, 193). Title 13 also provides the confidentiality guarantee for respondents.
- **Regulatory clearance:** Conducted under the Paperwork Reduction Act with **OMB control number 0607-1029**. The current approval expiration shown on the respondent page is **09/30/2028** (earlier ICR actions listed 01/31/2028). Key clearance milestones: initial HTOPS clearance January 15, 2025 (recruitment + Jan/Feb 2025 topical operations); April 11, 2025 (March–May collections); June 16, 2025 (June/August); September 24, 2025 (September–December); March 12, 2026 (2026 collections). Federal Register notices include the 60-day notice (88 FR 7681, Feb. 6, 2023) and 30-day notices (89 FR 97582, Dec. 9, 2024; 90 FR 10879; and subsequent 2025–2026 notices). Public comments were received on the ICRs.
- **Respondent obligation:** Voluntary. Contact: 1-888-595-1334, addp.htops@census.gov.

---

## 2. History and Provenance

| Period | Program/design |
|---|---|
| March 23 – April 23, 2020 | Household Pulse Survey designed in ~35 days as an emergency COVID-19 response |
| April 23, 2020 | HPS Phase 1 launches (OMB 0607-1013, emergency clearance); weekly data releases; partners: BLS, NCHS, HUD, NCES, USDA ERS |
| Aug 2020 – 2024 | HPS Phases 2 through 4.2, moving to regular OMB clearance (0607-1029), biweekly then monthly cadence; topics expand beyond COVID (inflation, childcare, energy, displacement, arts, etc.) |
| Sept–Oct 2023 | **Census Household Panel (CHP)** recruited (~15,000 households goal; OMB 0607-1025) as a probability-based methodological research panel; replenished March–April 2024 |
| Sept 16, 2024 | Cross-sectional HPS data collection ends; final release Oct 3, 2024 |
| Oct 2024 | HPS content begins transitioning to a **longitudinal design**, merged with the CHP |
| **January 2025** | **HTOPS officially launches**, relaunching HPS as a longitudinal panel; monthly-ish topical operations alternating HPS content with internal Census research (e.g., the September 2025 **2030 Census Planning Survey** — CBAMS-type content on census knowledge, trust, barriers, motivators); second replenishment Feb–Mar 2025 |
| **March 2026** | HTOPS transitions **from longitudinal back to cross-sectional design**, bi-monthly collections, ~136,000-household samples, to "support the production of estimates that meet quality standards of the Federal Statistical Agencies and OMB" |

The program's stated long-term ambition is to **graduate from an experimental data product to an official statistical product** as the methodology matures (per the December 2024 transition user note).

---

## 3. Methodology (current cross-sectional design)

- **Frame:** Census Bureau's **Master Address File (MAF)**, stratified using the Demographic Frame, the 2024 Block-Group Level Planning Database, and Community Resilience Estimates (social-vulnerability flags).
- **Sample size/calibration:** ~**136,000 housing units** per collection, sized to achieve a 9% coefficient of variation for a 15% population estimate in each of the 4 Census regions and the 10 largest CBSAs, assuming a ~10% response rate.
- **Mode:** Mail invitation with a link to an online questionnaire; up to 3 mailings; outbound/inbound CATI follow-up; CATI option preserves representation of non-internet households. (In the 2025 panel era, incentives were used: $5 prepaid at recruitment, $20 per completed questionnaire.)
- **Respondents:** ~12,600–12,800 completes per recent wave (July 2026: 12,755 of 136,094).
- **Response rates:** Low — **~9–10% unweighted** (July 2026: 9.4%; March 2026: 9.2%), a known limitation. Census has committed to a nonresponse bias analysis per OMB quality standards.
- **Weighting:** Base weights adjusted for nonresponse, adults per household, and coverage; supports national, regional, and top-10 CBSA estimates for adults 18+ in housing units (group quarters excluded).
- **Disclosure protection:** Title 13 confidentiality; Privacy Act; Disclosure Review Board approval (e.g., CBDRB-FY26-0334/-0351); individual items suppressed from public-use files when sample sizes pose disclosure risk (e.g., a naloxone-use item and an unemployment-insurance item were withheld from the May 2026 PUF).
- **Population:** U.S. adults 18+ in housing units, nationwide.

---

## 4. Content

Core demographics plus rotating topical modules. Topics documented across 2025–2026 waves include: employment and lost employment income; food sufficiency and dietary guidelines/consumer behavior; housing security, energy expenses, and pressure to move from rentals; health insurance (including Medicaid); mental health (including children's mental health treatment); K-12 enrollment and childcare; transportation; inflation concerns, price-change behavior, and difficulty paying usual expenses; household spending; access to infant formula; heat impacts; trust in health information; social isolation/connectedness; community and civic engagement; trust in government; shortage of critical items; arts participation (NEA); use of artificial intelligence; and 2030 Census attitudes (CBAMS-type modules).

---

## 5. Data Products and Access

- **Data tables:** Detailed tables per collection wave, published on the Household Pulse Survey data pages (HTOPS inherits the HPS dissemination infrastructure; waves use a "HTOPS HPS YYMM" naming convention, e.g., 2605 = May 2026). Geography: nation, 4 regions, top 10 metro areas. Tables show **frequency counts** including an unusual **"Did Not Report"** category (no imputation of missing values — users must choose denominators deliberately).
- **Public-use microdata files (PUFs):** Released per wave with data dictionaries.
- **Technical documentation:** Source-and-accuracy statements, user notes, questionnaires per wave.
- **Press releases and infographics:** e.g., March 26, April 23, and July 23, 2026 releases.
- **Known errata (important for preservationists and analysts):** The March and May 2026 PUFs and tables were **revised to correct a weighting error** — county-level population controls had included group quarters, misaligned with the HTOPS target population. Users must ensure they use corrected files, and archivists should capture both versions plus the user notes documenting the correction.
- **Not an API-fed series** in the way ACS/CPS are; dissemination is via file downloads on census.gov.
- **Status caveat:** Labeled an **experimental data product** — "designed to supplement the federal statistical system's traditional benchmark data products," not replace them.

---

## 6. Typical Users and Uses

- **Federal/state policymakers:** The HPS lineage was built to "help federal and state officials direct aid, assistance, and support to the people and places that need it most." During COVID, HPS data informed rental assistance, food assistance, eviction policy, and public-health response; partner agencies (e.g., CDC/NCHS for anxiety/depression indicators, USDA for food sufficiency, HUD for housing insecurity, NEA for arts participation, EIA for energy burden) sponsor and consume module data.
- **Census Bureau internally:** Survey-methods research, question-wording experiments, and 2030 Census planning (CBAMS successor content).
- **Researchers/academics:** Thousands of papers used HPS microdata on food insecurity, mental health, housing precarity, employment disruption, and childcare during and after the pandemic; HTOPS continues this role with bi-monthly cadence.
- **Journalists, advocates, and community organizations:** Near-real-time indicators on hardship, inflation stress, and health coverage — data "that cannot be collected elsewhere" at comparable speed.
- **State/local users:** Limited to national, regional, and top-10 CBSA geographies under the current design (state-level estimates were a feature of earlier HPS phases — a notable loss of granularity).

---

## 7. Benefits to the Public

1. **Speed:** Data released weeks after collection, versus months/years for benchmark surveys.
2. **Filling gaps:** Measures emergent issues (formula shortages, heat impacts, AI use, opioid-overdose reversal attempts) that no ongoing official survey covers.
3. **Equity lens:** Stratification on social vulnerability and oversampling design supports estimates for subgroups and high-need areas.
4. **Transparency:** Full public microdata, questionnaires, and accuracy statements; public comment opportunities via Federal Register notices.
5. **Statistical innovation:** A proving ground for methods (web-first, CATI fallback, MAF-based sampling, admin-record linkage) that improve the entire federal statistical system and the decennial census.

---

## 8. Limitations, Criticisms, and Cautions

- **Very low response rates** (~9–10%) raise nonresponse-bias concerns; the Census Bureau itself cautions against interpreting small differences and small-cell estimates, and has committed to formal nonresponse bias analysis.
- **Experimental status:** Estimates are not official statistics and carry explicit quality caveats; methods have changed frequently (weekly → biweekly → monthly cross-sectional → longitudinal → bi-monthly cross-sectional), creating **serious time-series comparability breaks**.
- **No imputation:** The "Did Not Report" convention shifts burden to users; naive percentage calculations can be misleading.
- **Geographic reduction:** Post-2024 designs dropped state-level and 15-metro detail to national/region/top-10 CBSA.
- **Documented data-quality incident:** The 2026 weighting-error correction demonstrates the risk of relying on uncorrected early releases.
- **Political/administrative vulnerability:** As a discretionary experimental collection renewed via short-cycle OMB clearances (waves approved a few months at a time), the program is more exposed to budget and policy shifts than statutorily mandated surveys.

---

## 9. Notes for Preservationists and Data Librarians

- **What to archive:** Per-wave PUFs (original and corrected versions), data dictionaries, questionnaires, source-and-accuracy statements, user notes (which carry critical errata), press releases, and the landing pages (which change with each redesign — the description you quoted has already been superseded on the live page).
- **Where it lives:** Dissemination is split between the HTOPS landing page (census.gov/programs-surveys/htops.html) and the legacy HPS pages (census.gov/programs-surveys/household-pulse-survey/*), with raw files under www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/demo/. This fragmentation plus the HPS→CHP→HTOPS→cross-sectional lineage makes provenance tracking essential.
- **Regulatory paper trail:** Federal Register notices (88 FR 7681; 89 FR 97582; 90 FR 10879; 2025-08397; 2026-02459; 2026-11172) and OMB reginfo/omb.report ICR records under control numbers 0607-1029 (HPS/HTOPS), 0607-1025 (CHP), and 0607-1013 (original HPS emergency clearance) are the authoritative record of mandate, burden, and design changes.
- **Predecessor data:** The complete HPS archive (2020–2024) and CHP topical files (2023–2024) should be preserved alongside HTOPS as one intellectual series.

---

## 10. Key Sources

- HTOPS landing page: https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/htops.html
- HPS/HTOPS data hub: https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/household-pulse-survey/data.html
- Source & Accuracy statements (2025–2026 waves): https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/demo/technical-documentation/hhp/
- Transition press release (Sept. 2024): https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024/longitudinal-design-household-pulse-survey.html
- HTOPS launch press release (2025): https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2025/household-trends-outlook-pulse-survey.html
- Federal Register notices: 88 FR 7681; 89 FR 97582 (Dec. 9, 2024); 90 FR 10879; 2025-08397 (May 13, 2025); 2025-15926 (Aug. 20, 2025); 2026-02459 (Feb. 9, 2026); 2026-11172 (June 4, 2026)
- OMB ICR record: https://omb.report/icr/202412-0607-001
- HPS background document (2020): https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/demo/technical-documentation/hhp/2020_HPS_Background.pdf
- HPS→HTOPS transition user note (Dec. 19, 2024): https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/demo/technical-documentation/hhp/October_2024_Household_Pulse_Survey_User_Notes_02062025.pdf

*Research note: Census.gov's HTML pages render heavily via JavaScript, so some landing-page details were verified through search-indexed excerpts of the same pages rather than full-page fetches; all substantive claims above are corroborated by Federal Register notices, OMB ICR records, and Census technical documentation.*

I'll research the current risk context for this dataset, including staffing, funding, policy actions, and any reported threats to Census Bureau surveys in 2025.I have strong evidence. Let me quickly verify two remaining points: whether the early-2025 Census data removals (including Household Pulse files) were restored, and the federal staffing tracker data for the Census Bureau.# Dataset Risk Assessment: Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey (HTOPS)

**Assessment date context:** Research conducted against evidence available through late 2025–2026, including Federal Register notices, OMB ICR records, FY2026 budget documents, and news reporting on Census Bureau operations under the second Trump administration.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence for Gone:** None — files are currently online.

**Evidence for High Risk:**
- In late January/early February 2025, in compliance with Executive Order 14168 and the January 29, 2025 OPM memo, "the Census Bureau's Household Pulse Survey (HPS) data and documentation had been deleted, and Census data could no longer be downloaded from the FTP site" (Williams Institute, UCLA Law, Feb. 2025; NPR Illinois, Feb. 12, 2025). The bureau's homepage itself went offline Jan. 31, 2025.
- This demonstrates the entire historical series (2020–present) has already been removed once, on days' notice, for ideological rather than technical reasons.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- Most data were restored following public outcry and the Feb. 11, 2025 court order in *Doctors for America v. OPM*; the Williams Institute notes "it is uncertain whether data that have been removed and restored temporarily will be permanently deleted."
- Data elements have been removed from the series: on Feb. 14, 2025 the Census Bureau requested OMB approval of a "non-substantive change" to **delete gender identity questions from HTOPS** (AP, Feb. 2025; NPR, Feb. 21, 2025). SOGI measures had been collected in HPS since 2021.
- The February 2025 HTOPS PUF "omitted select variables," requiring a separate supplemental file (census.gov datasets page).

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- As of this writing, HPS 2020–2024 PUFs, tables, and documentation and HTOPS 2025–2026 files are accessible at census.gov, including the 2024 and 2025 dataset pages.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** Historical files are currently intact, but this exact dataset was already taken offline once in 2025, and specific data elements (gender identity) have been prospectively removed with uncertain treatment in archived files. The demonstrated precedent of removal, plus restoration under legal duress rather than policy commitment, rules out "No Known Issue."

---

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence for Gone:** None — collection is active; March, May, and July 2026 waves were fielded and released.

**Evidence for High Risk:**
- DOGE announced in May 2025 it is reviewing "one-by-one" more than 100 Census Bureau surveys and had already "terminated" five it called wasteful (NPR, May 23, 2025; Washington Post, May 23, 2025). HTOPS is a discretionary, experimental collection of exactly the type targeted.
- The July 2025 collection was skipped ("The HTOPS program will not collect data in July to allow for operational updates," 90 FR, May 13, 2025).

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- HTOPS is approved in short tranches of 2–4 waves at a time (Jan 15, Apr 11, Jun 16, Sep 24, 2025; Mar 12, 2026), rather than a stable multi-year clearance — each tranche is an opportunity for non-renewal without any formal termination action.
- The design has changed three times in ~18 months (cross-sectional → longitudinal → cross-sectional), indicating programmatic instability.

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- ICR 0607-1029 is active; the respondent-facing approval shows expiration 09/30/2028. Waves in 2025–2026 were fielded and published on announced schedules, with press releases and revised files when needed.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** The ICR is active and publication has been timely, so "High Risk" is not yet met. But a skipped collection (July 2025), wave-by-wave clearance structure, and an active government-wide survey-termination review aimed at the Census Bureau make delayed or skipped future collection a realistic near-term possibility.

---

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence for High Risk:**
- **Granularity reduced:** The October 2024–January 2025 transition from HPS to HTOPS eliminated state-level estimates and the 15-metro detail, moving to national/4-region/top-10 CBSA only — a persistent reduction.
- **Frequency reduced:** HPS ran biweekly/monthly; HTOPS runs every other month, with a skipped month (July 2025).
- **Documented quality incident:** March and May 2026 PUFs and tables had to be revised to correct a weighting error (county population controls included group quarters, misaligned with the target population) — per 2026 user notes.
- **Content removed:** Gender identity items deleted (Feb. 2025); select variables omitted from the Feb. 2025 PUF; individual items suppressed from the May 2026 PUF for disclosure risk.
- Response rates of ~9–10% remain far below federal statistical norms; nonresponse bias analysis is still pending.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- The March 2026 return to a cross-sectional design was explicitly intended "to support the production of estimates that meet quality standards of the Federal Statistical Agencies and OMB," and sample sizes (~136,000) are large. Quality may stabilize or improve from here.

**Evidence for No Known Issue:** None — granularity and frequency are objectively below the predecessor series.

**Assessment: High Risk.** Reductions in granularity and frequency have actually occurred (not merely threatened) relative to the dataset's prior state, and a weighting error requiring reissue of official files is a concrete quality event. The rubric's High Risk definition — "reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency" — is squarely met.

---

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence for High Risk:**
- HTOPS is **not statutorily required**. It is conducted under general, discretionary Title 13 authorities (§§ 8(b), 131, 141, 182, 193, 196) — the same catch-all provisions cited for any Census survey. Nothing in statute names HTOPS, its content, or its schedule; it is self-described as an "experimental data product."
- **Substitutes exist:** CPS, ACS, SIPP, NHIS, and (until its own termination in September 2025) the USDA food-security module cover overlapping topics — employment, food sufficiency, housing, health insurance.
- **No dedicated programmatic mandate:** Partner agencies use the data, but no federal program's administration depends on HTOPS by law.
- Critically, the FY2026 President's Budget states the Census Bureau "will have eliminated functions that are not statutorily mandated or core to the Bureau's mission" (COSSA/Census Project analysis, June 2025) — language that describes HTOPS precisely.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk / No Known Issue:** Weak. The survey supports implementation of partner-agency missions (CDC, USDA, HUD, NEA modules), which gestures at the Moderate tier, but no program *requires* it, and the rubric's High Risk tier is explicitly met on all three prongs (vague authorization, available substitutes, no known statutory programmatic use).

**Assessment: High Risk.**

---

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence for High Risk:**
- **Leadership removed:** Director Rob Santos resigned in February 2025; the bureau has had no Senate-confirmed director since, with COO Ron Jarmin acting (AP, May 2025). This alone meets the High Risk threshold ("leadership removed").
- **1,000+ staff lost:** ~1,300 Census Bureau employees took deferred resignations, voluntary separations, or early retirement in 2025 (AFGE Council 241 president Johnny Zuagar, via AP/Washington Post, May 2025), out of ~13,230 employees (OPM, Sept. 2024) — roughly 10%, and the American Statistical Association's *The Nation's Data at Risk* (2025) estimates a **15% staffing loss since FY24**, with 18 of the top-leadership roster positions vacant and five+ division/office chiefs departed (NPR, April 2025).
- FY2026 President's Budget proposed cutting the **Current Surveys and Programs** account — which funds surveys like HTOPS — by **12.3%** (~$40M) (CRS IF12714; Census Project, June 2025).

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- The enacted FY2026 CJS bill (P.L. 119-74) softened this: Current Surveys funded at $319M, only ~3% below FY2025. Overall bureau funding rose due to decennial ramp-up.

**Evidence for No Known Issue:** None.

**Assessment: High Risk.** Two independent High Risk triggers are met: >1,000 staff lost and leadership removed. The 10–15% staffing decline also falls within the Moderate band, but the rubric's "and/or" structure makes High Risk unambiguous. (Note: the suggested USAJobs tracker at usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com renders data via JavaScript and could not be queried directly; it also tracks job *postings* rather than separations, and was archived Dec. 31, 2025. The AFGE/ASA/OPM figures above are the more direct evidence.)

---

## 6. Policy

**Evidence for High Risk:**
- **Presidential Action-driven ICR — the rubric's exact High Risk trigger:** On Feb. 14, 2025, the Census Bureau filed a non-substantive change request with OMB to delete gender identity questions from HTOPS, explicitly "to align with President Donald Trump's order" (EO 14168) (AP, Feb. 2025; NPR interview with former Director Santos, Feb. 21, 2025). KFF documents this as part of a government-wide SOGI data rollback affecting ~360 federal data collections (Williams Institute).
- **Negative policy action on site/data:** SOGI-related Census webpages were taken down (Boston Globe, Feb. 5, 2025), and HPS/HTOPS data files were temporarily deleted in Jan–Feb 2025.
- **Other significant changes per administration priorities:** DOGE's "survey of surveys" cost-cutting review (May 2025) with five surveys already terminated; the FY2026 budget's directive to eliminate non-statutory functions; the proposed reorganization merging Census with BLS and BEA (FY2026 CBJ).

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:** The ACS SOGI testing work was "suspended" pending clarification rather than formally killed — a pending change. But this is secondary.

**Evidence for No Known Issue:** None — multiple notable changes since January 2025 directly affect what this survey collects.

**Assessment: High Risk.** The Feb. 14, 2025 EO-driven ICR change to HTOPS itself is a textbook match for the rubric's High Risk criterion, and it is compounded by the temporary data deletion, the DOGE termination campaign, and budget language targeting non-statutory collections.

---

## Overall Summary

This dataset sits at the intersection of nearly every identified 2025–2026 risk vector for federal data: it is experimental and non-statutory (making it a stated target for elimination), it directly experienced an executive-order-driven content deletion and a temporary wholesale takedown, its sponsoring bureau has lost ~10–15% of staff and its director, and its granularity and frequency have already been reduced. Its main protective factors are an active multi-year ICR, continued on-schedule publication through mid-2026, congressional appropriators partially rejecting proposed survey-account cuts, and demonstrated public/legal pushback that restored deleted files. Preservation of the full HPS/CHP/HTOPS series — including original (pre-correction) 2026 files and pre-2025 questionnaires containing SOGI items — should be treated as urgent.
